strengths: The use of structured pruning in Eidetic Learning for addressing catastrophic forgetting is unique.
This theoretically sound solution offers clear guarantees for preventing forgetting.
Additionally, the authors plan to release a PyTorch framework, which will facilitate adoption and further experimentation by the research community.
Pruning is an approach in continual learning that makes sense, so it is good to further research it.
The experiments that are carried out make sense.
What is in the paper is well written, although some important information is missing.

Originality: The paper demonstrates a degree of originality by explicitly highlighting the importance of severing connections from reinitialized (previously pruned) neurons to frozen neurons crucial for prior tasks, which appears novel.

Quality: The paper presents a reasonably clear method with an intuitive justification for its ability to prevent forgetting, reports confidence intervals, and the commitment to releasing a PyTorch library enhances reproducibility.
Clarity: The paper is reasonably well-written and explains the Eidetic Learning procedure in a concise manner.
Significance: The paper addresses an important problem of catastrophic forgetting, has potential to influence future research, and the promised open-source library could contribute to adoption.
The introduction of Eidetic Learning provides a fresh perspective on addressing catastrophic forgetting by leveraging the concept of memory retention through structural network adjustments.
weaknesses: It only evaluates against other approaches on PMNIST and does not include comparisons with CIFAR-100 or Imagenette, making it hard to measure the true efficacy of Eidetic Learning.
There is no comparison using larger datasets like ImageNet-100 or Tiny ImageNet, making it impossible to assess how the method performs with datasets containing more than 10 classes.

The proposed method relies on task-id prediction to select the appropriate head, which may be infeasible without already being able to predict the class itself; the reviewer requests accuracy of the task predictor and comparison with class separation.

Several key elements of the paper (e.g., pruning method and task-id prediction) are barely explained, while other technical details are discussed at length; the reviewer suggests moving section 3.1 to the appendix and providing more explanation.
Important ablation results discussed in line 463 should be condensed and added to the main paper rather than being relegated to supplemental material.
The paper provides only limited comparison to similar methods (e.g., PackNet, Piggyback); differences are unclear and there is no proof that the proposed method works better than older methods.
The paragraph at line 349 contains spelling and grammar mistakes, and the referenced text about attention layers at the start of section 3 (line 291) appears to be missing.
The originality of the work is quite limited; prior work (e.g., “Compacting, Picking and Growing for Unforgetting Continual Learning”) proposes a similar mechanism.
The paper makes bold claims but provides limited experimental comparisons, evaluating on only one dataset, which falls short of standard experimentation quality.
The paper mentions making self-attention layers of Transformers immune to catastrophic forgetting, but does not provide the promised argument, appearing missing from the text.
It is unclear how the final task classifier can be trained on a meta task dataset without knowing the total number of tasks, raising questions about the experimental setup.
The claim of not requiring an additional hyperparameter search is questionable because the amount of pruning to tolerate accuracy drop is itself a hyper‑parameter to tune.
The paper contains numerous typographical and unclear statements (e.g., “seteting”, “a additional hyperparameter”, “An approach”, “we also need to pruning”, etc.).

The central claim that Eidetic Learning provably solves catastrophic forgetting is inaccurate/exaggerated; prior work already addresses the problem, and scalability concerns may limit the method’s completeness.
Limited experiments do not allow confirmation of a significant departure from state-of-the-art, as performance is statistically indistinguishable from prior work on only one dataset.
There is a lack of ablation study, recent baselines (post-2020), and information on the well‑time cost of the required EideticNet.
The authors do not conduct large‑scale experiments on ImageNet 1K or transformer‑based networks.
